title: ratatui
description: A Rust crate for cooking up terminal user interfaces (TUIs). Ratatui gives you immediate-mode widgets, flexible layout constraints, styling/colors, and pluggable backends (Crossterm by default) for building CLIs, dashboards, and full interactive console apps in pure Rust.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
# Getting Started

`ratatui` requires the Rust toolchain (this guide assumes you already have `rustc`/`cargo`
installed — on Arch Linux that's the `rust` package, e.g. `sudo pacman -S rust`, or `rustup`
if you want per-project toolchain management). This page only covers installing and
scaffolding **ratatui** itself.

## 1. Create a new binary crate

```bash
cargo new my-tui-app
cd my-tui-app
```

This gives you the standard layout:

```
my-tui-app/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    └── main.rs
```

## 2. Add ratatui and a backend

Ratatui doesn't talk to the terminal by itself — it renders into an in-memory buffer, and a
**backend** crate is what actually writes that buffer to the real terminal (handling raw
mode, cursor movement, colors, mouse/keyboard events, etc). The default and most portable
backend is [Crossterm](/ratatui/backends/), which works the same on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

```bash
cargo add ratatui crossterm
```

This adds both to `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
ratatui = "0.30"
crossterm = "0.29"
```

That's it — no system packages, no `apt`/`pacman` dependencies, ratatui is 100% pure Rust
with no C bindings by default when used with Crossterm.

## 3. (Optional) Scaffold from a template

If you don't want to hand-write the terminal setup/teardown boilerplate, Ratatui maintains
official templates via `cargo-generate`:

```bash
cargo install --locked cargo-generate
cargo generate ratatui/templates
```

You'll be prompted to choose a template (a minimal "simple" template, or a more structured
"component" template for larger apps — see [Project Structure](/ratatui/project-structure/)).
This guide builds everything by hand instead so you understand every piece, but the
templates are a legitimate shortcut once you know what they're doing for you.

## 4. Verify it builds

Paste the [Hello World](/ratatui/hello-world/) example from the next page into `src/main.rs`,
then:

```bash
cargo run
```

You should see `Hello World!` printed in an alternate terminal screen. Press any key to exit
back to your normal shell. If that works, your setup is complete — continue to
[Hello World](/ratatui/hello-world/) for a walkthrough of what just happened.

## Feature flags worth knowing about

Ratatui ships several optional Cargo features. You generally don't need to touch these for a
normal app, but they're worth knowing:

| Feature | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `crossterm` (default) | Enables the Crossterm backend. |
| `termion` | Alternative backend, Unix-only. |
| `termwiz` | Alternative backend used by the WezTerm project. |
| `serde` | Derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize` on layout/style types (`Constraint`, `Style`, `Color`, etc.) so you can save/load themes or layouts from disk. |
| `macros` | Enables the `ratatui-macros` convenience macros (e.g. `line!`, `text!`, `span!`). |
| `underline-color` | Enables setting a distinct underline color where the terminal supports it. |
| `layout-cache` | Caches layout computations; on by default with `std`, opt back in explicitly if you disable default features. |

Enable extras like this:

```bash
cargo add ratatui --features serde,macros
```

To disable the default Crossterm backend (e.g. to swap in `termion`):

```toml
ratatui = { version = "0.30", default-features = false, features = ["termion"] }
```
Getting Started.Choosing a Backend:
# Choosing a Backend

Ratatui doesn't talk to the terminal directly — it renders into a `Buffer` (a 2D grid of
styled cells), and a **backend** is responsible for diffing that buffer against the
previous frame and issuing the actual terminal escape codes. Ratatui ships three official
backend integrations, all optional via feature flags.

| Backend | Platforms | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Crossterm** (default) | Linux, macOS, Windows | Pure Rust, no C dependencies, actively maintained, widest compatibility. Use this unless you have a specific reason not to. |
| **Termion** | Unix-only (Linux, macOS, BSD) | Pure Rust, no Windows support, slightly different event API. |
| **Termwiz** | Cross-platform | Built for/by the WezTerm project; useful if you're already using Termwiz elsewhere. |

For essentially all new projects — including anything on Arch Linux — **Crossterm is the
right default**. It's what every current tutorial and template uses, has the largest
ecosystem of compatible crates, and is a pure-Rust dependency with no system libraries to
install.

```toml
[dependencies]
ratatui = "0.30"          # pulls in the crossterm backend by default
crossterm = "0.29"
```

## Switching backends

To use Termion instead:

```toml
ratatui = { version = "0.30", default-features = false, features = ["termion"] }
termion = "4"
```

Backend-specific color/key-event conversions live behind matching trait pairs, e.g. for
Crossterm:

```rust
use ratatui::style::Color;

let crossterm_color = crossterm::style::Color::Black;
let ratatui_color: Color = crossterm_color.into(); // or Color::from_crossterm(crossterm_color)
```

## The modular crate layout (0.30+)

Since ratatui 0.30, the project is split into a Cargo workspace so application authors and
widget-library authors depend on different amounts of it:

```
ratatui            (facade crate — re-exports everything, use this in apps)
├── ratatui-core        (fundamental traits: Widget, Buffer, Rect, Style...)
├── ratatui-widgets      (built-in widgets, depends on ratatui-core)
├── ratatui-crossterm    (Crossterm backend, depends on ratatui-core)
├── ratatui-termion      (Termion backend)
├── ratatui-termwiz      (Termwiz backend)
└── ratatui-macros       (line!/text!/span! macros)
```

**As an application author you should just depend on `ratatui` directly** — it re-exports
everything you need. The split mainly matters if you're publishing a third-party widget
crate and want to depend only on the slower-moving `ratatui-core` for better API stability
across ratatui versions.

```rust
// Application code — always do this:
use ratatui::widgets::{Widget, Block};

// Widget-library authors publishing their own crate might instead do:
use ratatui_core::widgets::Widget;
```

Layout.Layout Basics:
# Layout Basics

Ratatui has no concept of automatic reflow or CSS-like cascading — layout is explicit and
computed fresh every frame from a `Layout` object splitting a `Rect` into smaller `Rect`s.

## Rect

A `Rect` is just `{ x, y, width, height }` in terminal cells. `frame.area()` gives you the
`Rect` for the whole visible terminal.

## Layout::vertical / Layout::horizontal

```rust
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};

let [header, body, footer] = Layout::vertical([
    Constraint::Length(3),  // exactly 3 rows
    Constraint::Min(0),     // take all remaining space
    Constraint::Length(1),  // exactly 1 row
])
.areas(frame.area());

frame.render_widget("Header", header);
frame.render_widget("Body",   body);
frame.render_widget("Footer", footer);
```

`Layout::horizontal([...])` works the same way but splits left-to-right instead of
top-to-bottom. `.areas(rect)` returns a fixed-size array (the compiler checks the count
matches the number of constraints); use `.split(rect)` if you want a `Rc<[Rect]>` instead
(useful when the number of constraints isn't known until runtime).

## Constraint kinds

| Constraint | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Length(n)` | Exactly `n` cells. |
| `Min(n)` | At least `n` cells; grows to fill leftover space. |
| `Max(n)` | At most `n` cells. |
| `Percentage(p)` | `p`% of the parent area. |
| `Ratio(a, b)` | `a/b` of the parent area (avoids rounding drift `Percentage` can have across many splits). |
| `Fill(weight)` | Distributes remaining space proportionally to `weight` among all `Fill` constraints — the modern replacement for "give me whatever's left, split evenly." |

A typical three-pane layout — fixed header, flexible body split into two flexible columns,
fixed footer:

```rust
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};

let [header, body, footer] = Layout::vertical([
    Constraint::Length(3),
    Constraint::Min(0),
    Constraint::Length(1),
])
.areas(frame.area());

let [sidebar, main] = Layout::horizontal([
    Constraint::Fill(1),
    Constraint::Fill(3), // 3x wider than sidebar
])
.areas(body);
```

## Nesting layouts

Just call `Layout::...().areas(sub_rect)` again on any `Rect` you already split out — there's
no limit to how deeply you nest this. Each call is independent and cheap (results are
cached internally when the `layout-cache` feature is on, which it is by default).

## Rect helper methods (0.30+)

Newer convenience methods reduce boilerplate for common cases:

```rust
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Rect};

// Split directly on a Rect instead of calling .areas() on a Layout:
let [top, main] = area.layout(&Layout::vertical([Constraint::Length(3), Constraint::Min(0)]));

// Center a fixed-size box (e.g. for a dialog) within the full frame:
let popup = frame.area().centered(Constraint::Length(40), Constraint::Length(10));

// Center only along one axis:
let centered_row = frame.area().centered_horizontally(Constraint::Length(40));
```

See [Centering & Popups](/ratatui/centering-and-popups/) for the classic "centered modal
dialog" pattern this replaces.

## Margins, spacing, and padding

```rust
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Layout};

let layout = Layout::vertical([Constraint::Length(3), Constraint::Min(0)])
    .margin(1)      // 1 cell of margin on all sides of the whole layout
    .spacing(1);     // 1 cell gap *between* each split area
```

## Flex (how leftover space is distributed)

When your constraints don't add up to fill the whole area exactly, `Flex` controls where the
slack goes — this mirrors CSS flexbox fairly closely:

```rust
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Flex, Layout};

let layout = Layout::horizontal([Constraint::Length(10); 3]).flex(Flex::Center);
```

| Flex variant | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Start` (default) | Items packed at the start; slack goes at the end. |
| `End` | Items packed at the end; slack at the start. |
| `Center` | Items centered; equal slack on both sides. |
| `SpaceBetween` | Slack distributed evenly *between* items, none at the edges. |
| `SpaceAround` | Slack around each item; edge gaps are half the between-item gap. |
| `SpaceEvenly` | Slack distributed evenly between items *and* at both edges. |
| `Legacy` | Pre-0.26 behavior: all slack dumped at the end (kept for compatibility). |

Styling & Colors.Style Basics:
# Style Basics

Every renderable piece of text in ratatui (a `Span`, a `Line`, a widget's default text) can
carry a `Style`: foreground color, background color, and text modifiers (bold, italic,
underline, etc).

## Creating styles

```rust
use ratatui::style::{Color, Modifier, Style};

let style = Style::default()
    .fg(Color::Yellow)
    .bg(Color::Black)
    .add_modifier(Modifier::BOLD | Modifier::ITALIC);
```

## The Stylize shorthand trait (recommended)

Importing `ratatui::style::Stylize` adds fluent color/modifier methods directly onto
strings, `Span`s, `Line`s, and (as of 0.30) `Style` itself — this is the idiomatic way to
write styling in modern ratatui code and is what you'll see in almost every current example:

```rust
use ratatui::style::Stylize;

let span = "Error!".red().bold();
let span2 = "OK".green().on_black();
let span3 = "warning".yellow().italic().underlined();
```

As of 0.30, `Stylize` methods also work directly on `Style`, which lets you build style
constants without the verbose `Style::default().fg(...)` form:

```rust
use ratatui::style::Style;

const ERROR_STYLE: Style = Style::new().red().bold();
const HEADER_STYLE: Style = Style::new().white().on_blue();
```

## Modifiers

```rust
use ratatui::style::Modifier;
```

| Modifier | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `BOLD` | Bold text (terminal support varies). |
| `DIM` | Dimmed/faint text. |
| `ITALIC` | Italic (not supported by every terminal font/emulator). |
| `UNDERLINED` | Underline. |
| `SLOW_BLINK` / `RAPID_BLINK` | Blinking text — rarely used, poor support, often disabled by terminal emulators outright. |
| `REVERSED` | Swaps foreground and background. |
| `HIDDEN` | Invisible text (still occupies space). |
| `CROSSED_OUT` | Strikethrough. |

Combine with the bitwise-or operator: `Modifier::BOLD | Modifier::UNDERLINED`.

## Applying a style to a whole widget

Most widgets accept `.style(...)` to set a base style for their whole rendered area (which
individual `Span`s inside can still override):

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::Paragraph;
use ratatui::style::{Style, Color};

let paragraph = Paragraph::new("hello").style(Style::default().bg(Color::DarkGray));
```

## Style precedence

When styles overlap (e.g. a `Span`'s own style vs. the `Paragraph`'s base style vs. a
`Block`'s style), more specific styles win, and only the *set* fields override — an
unset `fg` on a `Span` doesn't blank out a `fg` set further up. This is why you can set a
background color on a whole `Block` and still have individual colored `Span`s show through
correctly on top of it.
Styling & Colors.Colors:
# Colors

`ratatui::style::Color` supports four different ways of specifying color, covering
everything from maximum terminal compatibility to full 24-bit precision.

## Named ANSI colors (most compatible)

The 16 standard terminal colors, guaranteed to render (with the terminal's own theme's exact
shades) on essentially every terminal emulator:

```rust
use ratatui::style::Color;

Color::Black;
Color::Red;
Color::Green;
Color::Yellow;
Color::Blue;
Color::Magenta;
Color::Cyan;
Color::Gray;       // "White" in some other libraries' naming
Color::DarkGray;
Color::LightRed;
Color::LightGreen;
Color::LightYellow;
Color::LightBlue;
Color::LightMagenta;
Color::LightCyan;
Color::White;
```

Use these when you want a TUI to look correct even on very old/minimal terminals (e.g. a
default TTY, or over a bare SSH session with no truecolor support).

## Color::Reset

`Color::Reset` explicitly resets to the terminal's default foreground/background instead of
picking a specific color — useful for "use whatever the user's theme default is" rather than
forcing a color.

## 256-color palette

```rust
Color::Indexed(202); // orange in the standard xterm 256-color palette
```

Wider palette than the 16 named colors, still broadly supported by modern terminals
(including virtually everything you'd use on Linux/Arch today — Alacritty, Kitty, WezTerm,
foot, GNOME Terminal, Konsole, etc).

## RGB / truecolor

```rust
Color::Rgb(255, 140, 0); // a specific shade of orange, exact on truecolor-capable terminals
```

Most terminals in current use support 24-bit truecolor, but not universally (some minimal or
legacy environments still don't) — if you need to support those, prefer the named ANSI
colors or 256-indexed colors, or detect and fall back.

## Conversions (0.30+)

Color can now be built directly from tuples and arrays, handy when values are coming from
elsewhere (a config file, a computed gradient) rather than written as literals:

```rust
use ratatui::style::Color;

let c1 = Color::from((255, 0, 0));       // same as Color::Rgb(255, 0, 0)
let c2 = Color::from([255, 0, 0]);
let c3 = Color::from((255, 0, 0, 255));  // RGBA tuple, alpha currently ignored by terminal output
```

Conversions from the `anstyle` crate's color types are also available behind the `anstyle`
Cargo feature, useful when integrating with other CLI tooling that already speaks `anstyle`.

## Picking a color strategy

- Building something you want to look right everywhere, including bare SSH sessions and old
  terminals → stick to the 16 named colors.
- Want a broader, still-safe palette → 256-indexed colors.
- Building a themeable app for modern terminal users (which describes almost everyone
  running Alacritty/Kitty/WezTerm on Linux) → `Color::Rgb` truecolor, with a documented
  fallback or a "basic colors" mode toggle if you want to support minimal terminals too.

## Background vs foreground

```rust
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};

let style = Style::default().fg(Color::White).bg(Color::Rgb(30, 30, 46)); // light text on dark bg
```

Or with `Stylize`: `"text".white().on_rgb(30, 30, 46)` — every named/indexed color has a
matching `.on_<color>()` background method (`.on_red()`, `.on_black()`, etc), and
`.on_rgb(r, g, b)` / `.on_indexed(n)` cover the rest.
Styling & Colors.Text, Spans, and Lines:
# Text, Spans, and Lines

Ratatui's text model is a small hierarchy that lets you mix styles within a single line, and
mix multiple lines within a block of text:

```
Text  (a whole block — Vec<Line>)
 └─ Line   (one row — Vec<Span>)
     └─ Span  (a run of same-styled text)
```

## Span — styled substring

```rust
use ratatui::text::Span;
use ratatui::style::Stylize;

let span = Span::styled("Error", ratatui::style::Style::new().red().bold());
let span2 = "Error".red().bold(); // shorthand via Stylize, produces the same Span
```

## Line — a row made of multiple Spans

```rust
use ratatui::text::Line;
use ratatui::style::Stylize;

let line = Line::from(vec![
    "Status: ".into(),
    "OK".green().bold(),
    " (".into(),
    "3 warnings".yellow().into(),
    ")".into(),
]);
```

`Line` also carries its own alignment:

```rust
use ratatui::layout::HorizontalAlignment; // renamed from `Alignment` in 0.30

let centered = Line::from("centered title").alignment(HorizontalAlignment::Center);
let right = Line::from("right-aligned").right_aligned(); // shorthand
```

## Text — multiple Lines

```rust
use ratatui::text::Text;

let mut text = Text::from("line 1");
text += Text::from("line 2"); // AddAssign, added in 0.30 — appends lines

let text2 = Text::from(vec![
    Line::from("Title").bold(),
    Line::from(""),
    Line::from("Body text goes here."),
]);
```

## Rendering text directly

Plain `&str`/`String`, `Span`, `Line`, and `Text` all implement `Widget` directly, so for
simple cases you don't need to wrap them in `Paragraph` at all:

```rust
frame.render_widget("plain text", area);
frame.render_widget(Line::from("styled").red(), area);
```

Wrap in `Paragraph` when you need wrapping, scrolling, or a surrounding `Block` — see
[Paragraph](/ratatui/paragraph-widget/).

## Measuring text width

As of 0.30, `Text`/`Line`/`Span` implement `UnicodeWidthStr`, so you can measure rendered
width directly (accounting for wide/CJK characters) instead of using `.len()`, which counts
bytes and will be wrong for anything non-ASCII:

```rust
use unicode_width::UnicodeWidthStr;

let width = line.width();      // display width
let width_cjk = line.width_cjk(); // width counting CJK characters as double-wide
```

This matters any time you're manually centering text or computing a `Constraint::Length`
from a string's contents — always measure display width, never `.len()`, once non-ASCII
text is possible.
Styling & Colors.Custom Themes:
# Custom Themes

There's no built-in "theme" type — a theme is just a plain struct of `Style`/`Color` values
that you define yourself and thread through your rendering code. This keeps ratatui
unopinionated but means the pattern is worth standardizing early in a project.

## A simple theme struct

```rust
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Theme {
    pub background: Color,
    pub foreground: Color,
    pub accent: Color,
    pub error: Color,
    pub warning: Color,
    pub success: Color,
    pub border: Color,
    pub border_focused: Color,
}

impl Theme {
    pub const DARK: Theme = Theme {
        background: Color::Rgb(24, 24, 37),
        foreground: Color::Rgb(205, 214, 244),
        accent: Color::Rgb(137, 180, 250),
        error: Color::Rgb(243, 139, 168),
        warning: Color::Rgb(249, 226, 175),
        success: Color::Rgb(166, 227, 161),
        border: Color::DarkGray,
        border_focused: Color::Rgb(137, 180, 250),
    };

    pub fn base_style(&self) -> Style {
        Style::new().fg(self.foreground).bg(self.background)
    }
}
```

Store an active `Theme` on your `App` struct and pass it (or fields of it) down into widget
constructors during `draw`.

## Loading themes from config (serde)

Enable the `serde` feature and most style/layout types (`Color`, `Style`, `Constraint`,
`Modifier`, etc.) can be (de)serialized directly, so themes can live in a TOML/JSON config
file instead of being hardcoded:

```bash
cargo add ratatui --features serde
cargo add serde --features derive
cargo add toml
```

```rust
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct ThemeConfig {
    background: ratatui::style::Color,
    foreground: ratatui::style::Color,
    accent: ratatui::style::Color,
}

let config: ThemeConfig = toml::from_str(&std::fs::read_to_string("theme.toml")?)?;
```

```toml
# theme.toml
background = { type = "Rgb", red = 24, green = 24, blue = 37 }
foreground = "White"
accent = { type = "Indexed", 0 = 39 }
```

(Exact serde field shapes depend on how `Color`'s variants derive — check the shape by
serializing a default value once with `serde_json::to_string` and using that as your
reference, since indexed/tuple variant JSON shapes vary between serde-derived enums.)

## Light/dark toggle

Keep two `Theme` constants and swap which one your `App` points to on a keybinding — since
`Theme` is just data, this is a plain field swap, no re-render logic needed beyond your
normal `draw` already reading from `app.theme`.

Widgets.Widgets Overview:
# Widgets Overview

A **widget** in ratatui is anything implementing the `Widget` trait — essentially, anything
that knows how to draw itself into a `Rect` of a `Buffer`. Because rendering is immediate
mode (see [Rendering & the Frame Loop](/ratatui/rendering/)), widgets are cheap, short-lived
builder objects you construct fresh each frame from your app's state, not long-lived objects
you mutate in place.

## Stateless vs stateful widgets

Most built-in widgets (`Paragraph`, `Block`, `Tabs`, `Gauge`, `BarChart`, `Sparkline`,
`Chart`, `Canvas`) are **stateless**: you build them fully from data each frame and render
with `frame.render_widget(widget, area)`.

A few widgets need to remember something across frames that isn't naturally part of your own
app state — most commonly *which item is currently selected/scrolled to*. These are
**stateful widgets**: `List`, `Table`, and `Scrollbar`. You own a small `*State` struct
(`ListState`, `TableState`, `ScrollbarState`) on your `App`, and render with
`frame.render_stateful_widget(widget, area, &mut state)` instead.

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::{List, ListState};

let list = List::new(["Item 0", "Item 1", "Item 2"]);
frame.render_stateful_widget(list, area, &mut app.list_state); // app.list_state: ListState
```

## The built-in widget catalog

| Widget | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Block` | Border/title container wrapping other widgets. |
| `Paragraph` | Wrapped, styled, scrollable text. |
| `List` | Selectable vertical list of items. |
| `Table` | Rows/columns with headers, selectable rows. |
| `Tabs` | A horizontal row of tab labels. |
| `Gauge` / `LineGauge` | Progress bars (block-filled or line-style). |
| `BarChart` | Vertical/horizontal/grouped bar charts. |
| `Sparkline` | Compact single-line data trend. |
| `Chart` | Full XY line/scatter charts with axes and legends. |
| `Scrollbar` | Visual scroll position indicator. |
| `Calendar` | Month calendar grid, via the `widgets::calendar` module (needs the `time` crate). |
| `Canvas` | Freeform vector drawing (lines, shapes, maps) using braille/block characters. |
| `Clear` | Utility widget that blanks an area — used under popups. |
| `RatatuiMascot` | The ratatui logo/mascot as a widget (added in 0.30 — mostly for fun/demos). |

Every widget's page in this doc includes its constructor, its common builder methods, and a
runnable example.

## Composing widgets

Widgets nest via layout, not via a parent/child API — you split a `Rect` with
[Layout](/ratatui/layout-basics/), then render a different widget into each resulting
sub-`Rect`. `Block` is the exception: it has an `.inner(area)` method returning the `Rect`
*inside* its own borders, which is how you nest other widgets visually inside a bordered box
(see [Block](/ratatui/block-widget/)).

## Custom widgets

If none of the built-ins fit, implement `Widget` yourself — see
[Building Custom Widgets](/ratatui/custom-widgets/).
Widgets.Block:
# Block

`Block` draws a border and/or title around an area, and is almost always used as a wrapper
around another widget rather than standalone.

## Basic usage

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::{Block, Borders};

let block = Block::default()
    .title("My Panel")
    .borders(Borders::ALL);

frame.render_widget(block, area);
```

Shorthand for the common "border on all sides" case:

```rust
let block = Block::bordered().title("My Panel");
```

## Border sides and types

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::{Block, Borders, BorderType};

Block::default().borders(Borders::TOP | Borders::BOTTOM); // only top and bottom
Block::bordered().border_type(BorderType::Rounded);        // rounded corners: ╭─╮
Block::bordered().border_type(BorderType::Double);         // double lines: ╔═╗
Block::bordered().border_type(BorderType::Thick);          // heavy lines: ┏━┓
```

0.30 added several dashed border styles for a lighter, more subtle look:
`BorderType::LightDoubleDashed`, `HeavyDoubleDashed`, `LightTripleDashed`,
`HeavyTripleDashed`, `LightQuadrupleDashed`, `HeavyQuadrupleDashed`.

## Titles

As of 0.30, `Block::title()` takes anything convertible into a `Line` directly (the old
`block::Title` type was removed) — so title alignment is set on the `Line` itself:

```rust
use ratatui::text::Line;
use ratatui::style::Stylize;

let block = Block::bordered()
    .title(Line::from(" My Panel ").centered())
    .title(Line::from(" v1.0 ").right_aligned().dim());
```

You can attach multiple titles (e.g. one left-aligned, one right-aligned) by calling
`.title(...)` more than once.

## Styling the block itself

```rust
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};

let block = Block::bordered()
    .style(Style::default().bg(Color::Black))       // background fill of the whole block
    .border_style(Style::default().fg(Color::Cyan)); // color of just the border characters
```

## Nesting a widget inside a Block

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::{Block, Paragraph};

let block = Block::bordered().title("Log");
let inner_area = block.inner(area); // the Rect *inside* the border
frame.render_widget(block, area);
frame.render_widget(Paragraph::new("log contents..."), inner_area);
```

Or attach the block directly to a widget that supports `.block(...)` (most do, including
`Paragraph`, `List`, `Table`):

```rust
let paragraph = Paragraph::new("log contents...").block(Block::bordered().title("Log"));
frame.render_widget(paragraph, area);
```

## Padding

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::Padding;

let block = Block::bordered().padding(Padding::uniform(1)); // 1 cell of space inside the border
```

## Collapsing/merging adjacent borders (0.30+)

When two bordered `Block`s sit directly adjacent, their shared edge can visually merge into
clean T/cross junctions instead of drawing two overlapping border lines. This is handled
automatically by the renderer's border-merging logic as of 0.30 — see the
[Collapsed Borders](https://ratatui.rs/examples/widgets/collapsed-borders/) example for the
exact grid layouts this applies to.
Widgets.Gauge and LineGauge:
# Gauge and LineGauge

Two different visual styles of progress indicator: `Gauge` fills a solid block area, while
`LineGauge` renders a single line using fill/track characters.

## Gauge

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::Gauge;
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};

let gauge = Gauge::default()
    .block(ratatui::widgets::Block::bordered().title("Progress"))
    .gauge_style(Style::default().fg(Color::Green).bg(Color::Black))
    .ratio(0.42) // 0.0 to 1.0
    .label("42%");
```

`ratio(0.0..=1.0)` is the fraction filled; `percent(0..=100)` is equivalent using a whole
number instead. `.label(...)` overrides the default auto-generated percentage label — pass
an empty string to hide the label entirely.

## LineGauge

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::LineGauge;
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};

let gauge = LineGauge::default()
    .filled_style(Style::default().fg(Color::Cyan))
    .ratio(0.80);
```

As of 0.30, the fill/track characters themselves are customizable directly (the older
`.line_set(...)` symbol-set method is now deprecated in favor of this):

```rust
let gauge = LineGauge::default()
    .filled_symbol("█")
    .unfilled_symbol("░")
    .ratio(0.80);
```

producing something like:

```
80% ████████████░░░░
```

## Animating a gauge (progress over time)

Since ratatui has no built-in animation/tween system, "animating" a gauge just means
updating the underlying value (e.g. download progress, a loading spinner's ratio) in your
tick handler and re-rendering — see [Animations & Effects](/ratatui/animations-and-effects/)
for the general pattern, and for smoother eased transitions via the third-party `tachyonfx`
crate.
Widgets.Chart:
# Chart

`Chart` is the full XY plotting widget: multiple labeled datasets, axes with custom bounds
and labels, and an optional legend. Use this over `BarChart`/`Sparkline` when you need actual
line/scatter plots with numeric axes rather than a simple bar/trend display.

## Basic usage

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::{Axis, Chart, Dataset, GraphType};
use ratatui::style::{Color, Style};
use ratatui::symbols;
use ratatui::text::Span;

let data: Vec<(f64, f64)> = (0..50).map(|x| {
    let x = x as f64;
    (x, x.sin())
}).collect();

let dataset = Dataset::default()
    .name("sin(x)")
    .marker(symbols::Marker::Braille)
    .graph_type(GraphType::Line)
    .style(Style::default().fg(Color::Cyan))
    .data(&data);

let chart = Chart::new(vec![dataset])
    .block(ratatui::widgets::Block::bordered().title("Waveform"))
    .x_axis(
        Axis::default()
            .title(Span::styled("x", Style::default().fg(Color::Gray)))
            .bounds([0.0, 50.0])
            .labels(vec!["0".into(), "25".into(), "50".into()]),
    )
    .y_axis(
        Axis::default()
            .title(Span::styled("y", Style::default().fg(Color::Gray)))
            .bounds([-1.0, 1.0])
            .labels(vec!["-1".into(), "0".into(), "1".into()]),
    );

frame.render_widget(chart, area);
```

## Multiple datasets + legend

```rust
let chart = Chart::new(vec![dataset_a, dataset_b])
    .legend_position(Some(ratatui::widgets::LegendPosition::TopRight));
```

## GraphType

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::GraphType;
```

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Scatter` | Individual points, no connecting line. |
| `Line` | Points connected with straight line segments. |
| `Bar` | Vertical bars from the x-axis up to each point. |

## Marker resolution

`symbols::Marker` controls what characters are used to plot points — `Braille` gives the
highest resolution (multiple sub-pixels per terminal cell) and is the default; `Dot`/`Block`
are lower-resolution but more universally supported. 0.30 added `Quadrant`, `Sextant`, and
`Octant` as additional high-resolution options between `Block` and `Braille` — see
[Canvas](/ratatui/canvas-widget/) for the full marker comparison, since `Chart` and `Canvas`
share the same marker system.

## Live-updating charts

Push new `(x, y)` points onto a `VecDeque`/`Vec` on tick, drop old ones past some window size,
and rebuild the `Dataset` from current data each frame — there's no persistent chart state to
update in place, consistent with ratatui's immediate-mode rendering.
Widgets.Canvas:
# Canvas

`Canvas` is ratatui's freeform vector-drawing widget: lines, rectangles, circles, and
arbitrary points plotted onto a continuous coordinate space, rendered using
high-resolution terminal characters (braille, block, or quadrant/sextant/octant symbols)
rather than being restricted to whole terminal cells.

## Basic usage

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::canvas::{Canvas, Line as CanvasLine, Rectangle};
use ratatui::style::Color;

let canvas = Canvas::default()
    .block(ratatui::widgets::Block::bordered().title("Canvas"))
    .x_bounds([-100.0, 100.0])
    .y_bounds([-100.0, 100.0])
    .paint(|ctx| {
        ctx.draw(&CanvasLine {
            x1: -50.0, y1: 0.0,
            x2: 50.0, y2: 0.0,
            color: Color::Yellow,
        });
        ctx.draw(&Rectangle {
            x: -20.0, y: -20.0,
            width: 40.0, height: 40.0,
            color: Color::Cyan,
        });
    });

frame.render_widget(canvas, area);
```

`.x_bounds([min, max])` / `.y_bounds([min, max])` define the logical coordinate space that
gets mapped onto the widget's actual terminal-cell area — this lets you draw in whatever
units make sense for your data (e.g. real map coordinates) without manually converting to
cell positions.

## Points and shapes

```rust
use ratatui::widgets::canvas::Points;
use ratatui::style::Color;

ctx.draw(&Points {
    coords: &[(0.0, 0.0), (10.0, 10.0), (20.0, 5.0)],
    color: Color::Red,
});
```

Also available: `Circle`, `Map` (a rough world map outline, useful for geo-themed dashboards),
and you can implement the `Shape` trait yourself for custom drawing primitives.

## Marker resolution

```rust
use ratatui::symbols::Marker;

let canvas = Canvas::default().marker(Marker::Braille); // default; highest resolution
```

| Marker | Resolution per cell | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Dot` | 1x1 | Lowest resolution, most universally supported. |
| `Block` | 1x1 (solid) | Filled block per cell. |
| `Bar` | 1x1 (half-height) | Half-block characters. |
| `Braille` | 2x4 | Default; widest terminal support for this resolution. |
| `Quadrant` (0.30+) | 2x2 | Densely packed, no visible banding between cells. |
| `Sextant` (0.30+) | 2x3 | Higher resolution than Quadrant; less universally supported. |
| `Octant` (0.30+) | 2x4 | Same resolution as Braille but with denser, more regular pseudo-pixels; least widely supported font-wise. |

For maximum compatibility (including older terminals or unusual fonts on a minimal Arch
setup), stick with `Braille` or `Dot`. For visually denser plots on modern terminals with
good Unicode font coverage, `Quadrant`/`Sextant`/`Octant` are worth trying, with `Braille` as
an automatic fallback path if you detect rendering issues.

## Interactive drawing (mouse)

Combine `Canvas` with mouse events (see [Handling Input](/ratatui/handling-input/)) to build
freeform drawing apps — translate the mouse's terminal-cell `(column, row)` into your
canvas's logical coordinate space using the same bounds you passed to `.x_bounds()`/
`.y_bounds()`, then push a new shape into your app's draw buffer and redraw.

Rendering & Performance.Rendering & the Frame Loop:
# Rendering & the Frame Loop

Ratatui is built on **immediate-mode rendering with an intermediate buffer** — understanding
this model explains most of the library's API shape.

## What "immediate mode" means here

Every call to `terminal.draw(|frame| { ... })` must describe the *entire* UI from scratch:
every widget that should be visible this frame gets rendered inside that one closure, based
on your app's current state. There's no persistent widget tree living across frames that you
mutate in place (contrast with "retained mode" GUI toolkits, where you build a tree once and
then update individual nodes).

```rust
terminal.draw(|frame| {
    // This entire closure runs on every single frame, describing the whole UI each time.
    frame.render_widget(&app, frame.area());
})?;
```

This is simpler to reason about (the UI is a pure function of state, evaluated fresh each
time) at the cost of doing more work per frame than a retained-mode system technically needs
— though in practice this cost is negligible for terminal UIs at typical refresh rates.

## The double-buffer diff

Under the hood, `Terminal` keeps two `Buffer`s: the one you just rendered into, and the one
from the previous frame. After your closure returns, ratatui **diffs** the two buffers and
only sends terminal escape codes for the cells that actually changed — not the whole screen.
This is why ratatui apps don't flicker even at high refresh rates: unchanged parts of the
screen generate zero terminal writes.

## Cursor position

Ratatui doesn't render a cursor by default. If you're building a text input, explicitly
position it inside your draw closure:

```rust
frame.set_cursor_position((input_area.x + app.cursor_col, input_area.y));
```

Call this only when you actually want the terminal's blinking cursor visible (e.g. inside a
focused text field) — omit it on frames where no input widget is focused.

## Frame vs Terminal

- `Terminal` owns the backend and the double-buffer; you call `terminal.draw(...)` on it once
  per frame.
- `Frame` is the short-lived handle passed into your draw closure — it's what you call
  `.render_widget(...)`, `.area()`, and `.set_cursor_position(...)` on. It only exists for the
  duration of one `draw` call.

## Redraw only when needed (efficiency, not correctness)

Because of the buffer diff, calling `terminal.draw` when nothing changed is cheap but not
free — it still walks and diffs the whole buffer. For very tight ticking loops (high-FPS
animations), it's common to track a `needs_redraw: bool` on `App`, set it whenever state
actually changes, and only call `terminal.draw` when it's true — resetting it to false right
after. This is a performance optimization, not something required for correct rendering.
Rendering & Performance.Debugging:
# Debugging

Debugging a full-screen terminal app is awkward in the obvious way: `println!`/`dbg!` output
gets immediately overwritten or corrupted by the alternate-screen UI. Here's what actually
works.

## Never println! while the alternate screen is active

Any `println!`/`eprintln!`/`dbg!` call while your app is in the alternate screen (i.e.
between `ratatui::init()` and `ratatui::restore()`) writes garbage into your rendered UI, not
a clean line of output. Avoid it entirely during that window.

## Logging to a file with `tracing`

The standard approach is to log to a file instead of stdout/stderr, then `tail -f` that file
in a separate terminal pane while your TUI runs in another:

```bash
cargo add tracing tracing-subscriber tracing-appender
```

```rust
fn init_logging() -> tracing_appender::non_blocking::WorkerGuard {
    let file_appender = tracing_appender::rolling::never(".", "debug.log");
    let (writer, guard) = tracing_appender::non_blocking(file_appender);
    tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_writer(writer).with_ansi(false).init();
    guard // keep this alive for the lifetime of main()
}

fn main() -> color_eyre::Result<()> {
    let _guard = init_logging();
    tracing::info!("app starting");
    // ... normal ratatui::init()/run/restore ...
}
```

Then, in a second terminal:

```bash
tail -f debug.log
```

This gives you real-time, non-corrupting visibility into what your app is doing while the TUI
is on screen in the first terminal.

## Panic hooks (don't lose the message)

A panic inside `terminal.draw` or your event loop, without a restoring panic hook, both
leaves the terminal in raw/alternate-screen mode *and* can make the panic message impossible
to read once the terminal state is restored by hand. `ratatui::init()` already installs a
hook that restores the terminal before the default panic message prints (see
[Terminal Setup](/ratatui/terminal-setup/)); pairing it with `color_eyre` additionally makes
that message a well-formatted backtrace instead of Rust's default panic output.

## Debugging widget state visually

Sometimes the fastest way to understand a layout/rendering bug is to render debug
information as part of the UI itself — e.g. temporarily rendering a widget's computed `Rect`
coordinates, or an app's raw state struct via `{:#?}`, into a corner of the screen:

```rust
let debug_text = format!("{:#?}", app.list_state);
frame.render_widget(
    ratatui::widgets::Paragraph::new(debug_text),
    ratatui::layout::Rect::new(0, 0, 40, 10),
);
```

Gate this behind a keybinding or a `debug_mode: bool` flag on `App` so it's easy to toggle on
only when needed, and strip it (or leave it dev-only) before release.

## rust-analyzer / breakpoint debugging

Because `terminal.draw` takes over the terminal, running your program under a normal
interactive debugger (`gdb`, `lldb`, or an IDE debugger) works fine for setting breakpoints
in your update/event-handling logic — just be aware that hitting a breakpoint *while* the
alternate screen is active will freeze your terminal in that state until you resume or detach,
since nothing is around to call `ratatui::restore()` for you mid-breakpoint.

## Common bugs and their causes

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Terminal left garbled/raw after app exits | Missing `ratatui::restore()` on some exit path (e.g. `std::process::exit`, or an unhandled panic without a hook installed). |
| Actions fire twice per keypress | Not filtering for `KeyEventKind::Press` — see [Handling Input](/ratatui/handling-input/). |
| Popup shows leftover characters underneath | Forgot to render `Clear` before the popup — see [Centering & Popups](/ratatui/centering-and-popups/). |
| Layout looks wrong only with non-ASCII text | Using `.len()` instead of `UnicodeWidthStr::width()` to measure text — see [Text, Spans, and Lines](/ratatui/text-spans-and-lines/). |
| App is unresponsive to input while animating | Using blocking `event::read()` instead of `event::poll(timeout)` — see [The Elm-Style App Loop](/ratatui/the-elm-style-app-loop/). |
Rendering & Performance.Performance Tips:
# Performance Tips

Ratatui is fast by default for the overwhelming majority of apps — these tips matter mainly
for very large datasets (thousands of rows), very high tick rates, or resource-constrained
environments.

## Let the buffer diff do its job

Don't try to manually skip `terminal.draw()` calls as a performance hack unless you've
actually measured a problem — the double-buffer diff (see
[Rendering & the Frame Loop](/ratatui/rendering/)) already ensures unchanged cells generate
zero terminal writes. Premature "only redraw if dirty" logic mostly adds bug surface for
little real benefit at normal UI sizes.

## Avoid recomputing expensive data inside draw

`draw` should stay cheap and read-only. If a data transformation is expensive (parsing,
filtering thousands of items, recomputing a chart's dataset), do it once when the underlying
data changes (in your update/tick step) and cache the *result* on `App`, rather than
recomputing it from scratch every single frame inside `draw`.

```rust
// Bad: recomputes every frame even if nothing changed.
fn draw(&self, frame: &mut Frame) {
    let filtered: Vec<_> = self.all_items.iter().filter(|i| i.matches(&self.query)).collect();
    // ...
}

// Better: recompute only when query/items actually change.
fn on_query_changed(&mut self) {
    self.filtered_items = self.all_items.iter().filter(|i| i.matches(&self.query)).cloned().collect();
}
```

## Layout cache

The `layout-cache` feature (on by default when using `std`) caches `Layout::split` results
keyed by input, so repeatedly computing the same layout split (e.g. the same three-pane
layout every frame) is effectively free after the first call. If you've disabled default
features for a `no_std`/embedded target and still have `std` available, re-enable it
explicitly:

```toml
ratatui = { version = "0.30", default-features = false, features = ["layout-cache"] }
```

## Large lists/tables

`List`/`Table` only render the rows currently visible in their `area` — you don't need to
manually paginate or windows a `Vec` of thousands of items yourself; just pass the whole
collection in and let `ListState`/`TableState`'s scroll offset determine which slice is drawn
each frame.

## Truecolor vs indexed color cost

There's no meaningful rendering-speed difference between `Color::Rgb`, `Color::Indexed`, and
the named ANSI colors — the cost of color choice is entirely about terminal *compatibility*
(see [Colors](/ratatui/colors/)), not performance.

## Reduce tick rate when idle

If your app has an idle animation (a spinner, a clock) that only matters while visible and
nothing else is happening, there's no need to tick at 60fps constantly — dropping to a lower
idle tick rate (e.g. 4-10 ticks/sec) when there's no active animation running noticeably
reduces CPU usage for long-running background TUIs (dashboards, monitors) with negligible
visual difference.

Shipping.Building for Release:
# Building for Release

Standard Cargo release build — nothing ratatui-specific is required, but a few flags are
worth knowing for shipping a polished CLI/TUI binary.

## Basic release build

```bash
cargo build --release
```

The optimized binary lands at `target/release/<crate-name>`.

## Cargo.toml release profile tuning

For a small, fast binary (worth it for something users will `pacman -U` or download as a
prebuilt binary):

```toml
[profile.release]
opt-level = 3       # or "s"/"z" to optimize for size instead of speed
lto = true          # link-time optimization, smaller & sometimes faster binary, slower build
codegen-units = 1   # better optimization at the cost of build parallelism
strip = true        # strip debug symbols from the final binary
panic = "abort"     # smaller binary; disables unwinding (fine for most CLI/TUI apps)
```

`panic = "abort"` means a panic immediately aborts the process rather than unwinding — this
is usually fine for a TUI app (you're going to `ratatui::restore()` in a panic hook either
way, and an abort still runs that hook first), but skip it if anything in your dependency
tree specifically requires catching panics with `catch_unwind`.

## Cross-compiling

Ratatui and Crossterm are both pure Rust, so cross-compilation works the same as any other
Rust project — install the target and build:

```bash
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl   # e.g. for a static Linux binary
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
```

A `musl` target is worth considering for a TUI you're distributing as a single binary to
users on unknown Linux distros — it statically links libc, avoiding glibc-version mismatches
entirely.

## Verifying the terminal-restore behavior in a release build

Before shipping, explicitly test: quitting normally, `Ctrl+C` during startup, `Ctrl+C`
mid-render, and triggering a deliberate panic (e.g. an `unwrap()` on bad input) — confirm the
terminal is left in a clean, usable state after every one of these, since a debug-build test
pass doesn't guarantee optimized-build panic-unwind behavior is identical, especially with
`panic = "abort"` set.
Shipping.Packaging for Arch Linux:
# Packaging for Arch Linux

Since ratatui and Crossterm are pure Rust with no system library dependencies, packaging a
ratatui app for Arch is exactly the same as packaging any other Rust binary — no special
handling required for the TUI parts.

## Minimal PKGBUILD

```bash
# Maintainer: psdk
pkgname=my-tui-app
pkgver=0.1.0
pkgrel=1
pkgdesc="A terminal UI built with ratatui"
arch=('x86_64')
url="https://github.com/psdk/my-tui-app"
license=('MIT')
depends=()
makedepends=('cargo')
source=("$pkgname-$pkgver.tar.gz::https://github.com/psdk/my-tui-app/archive/v$pkgver.tar.gz")
sha256sums=('SKIP')

prepare() {
    cd "$pkgname-$pkgver"
    cargo fetch --locked
}

build() {
    cd "$pkgname-$pkgver"
    cargo build --frozen --release
}

package() {
    cd "$pkgname-$pkgver"
    install -Dm755 "target/release/$pkgname" "$pkgdir/usr/bin/$pkgname"
}
```

`depends=()` is correct and important here: because ratatui + Crossterm are pure Rust with no
FFI to a system TUI library (no `ncurses`, no `libtinfo`), the resulting binary has no
runtime dependency beyond glibc, which is already a base-system dependency and doesn't need
listing.

## Local install/test without the AUR

```bash
makepkg -si
```

builds and installs the package locally, useful for testing the PKGBUILD before publishing
to the AUR.

## Publishing to the AUR

```bash
git clone ssh://aur@aur.archlinux.org/my-tui-app.git
cd my-tui-app
cp /path/to/PKGBUILD .
makepkg --printsrcinfo > .SRCINFO
git add PKGBUILD .SRCINFO
git commit -m "Initial import"
git push
```

## Terminfo considerations

Crossterm talks to the terminal via ANSI escape codes directly rather than reading
`terminfo`/`termcap` entries, so there's no `ncurses`/`terminfo` database dependency to worry
about — a ratatui app should behave identically across Arch's common terminal emulators
(Alacritty, Kitty, foot, WezTerm, GNOME Terminal, Konsole) without any terminal-specific
packaging steps.
Shipping.Distributing Cross-Platform:
# Distributing Cross-Platform

Because ratatui's default Crossterm backend is cross-platform pure Rust, the same codebase
runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows without conditional compilation for the TUI layer itself —
platform differences mostly show up in build tooling and terminal capability detection, not
in ratatui's own API.

## GitHub Actions release build matrix

A typical release workflow builds each target and attaches binaries to a GitHub Release:

```yaml
name: Release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
            os: ubuntu-latest
          - target: x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
            os: ubuntu-latest
          - target: x86_64-apple-darwin
            os: macos-latest
          - target: aarch64-apple-darwin
            os: macos-latest
          - target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
            os: windows-latest
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}
      - run: cargo build --release --target ${{ matrix.target }}
```

## publishing to crates.io

If your app is also useful as a library, or you simply want `cargo install my-tui-app` to
work for anyone with a Rust toolchain regardless of OS:

```bash
cargo login
cargo publish --dry-run   # sanity check first
cargo publish
```

Users can then install directly:

```bash
cargo install my-tui-app
```

This sidesteps platform-specific binary distribution entirely, at the cost of requiring the
Rust toolchain on the user's machine.

## Terminal capability differences to test for

- **Windows Terminal / ConPTY** vs legacy `cmd.exe`: legacy consoles have weaker ANSI/color
  support; Windows Terminal handles truecolor and most modifiers fine.
- **True color support** varies across less common terminal emulators — provide a fallback
  or a config option to force 16/256-color mode if you're targeting unknown environments (see
  [Colors](/ratatui/colors/)).
- **Font/Unicode coverage** for box-drawing and Braille characters can differ, particularly
  on Windows with older fonts — test `BorderType::Rounded`/`Double` and `Canvas`'s
  `Marker::Braille` specifically, since these rely on less universally-covered Unicode
  ranges than plain ASCII box characters.

## Homebrew / winget / AUR as convenience installers

Once you have release binaries, a Homebrew formula (macOS), a `winget`/Scoop manifest
(Windows), and an AUR package (Arch — see
[Packaging for Arch Linux](/ratatui/packaging-for-arch-linux/)) are the standard trio for
letting users install without touching Cargo or GitHub Releases directly.
Shipping.The Ratatui Ecosystem:
# The Ratatui Ecosystem

A short map of notable crates that extend ratatui beyond what ships in the core library,
useful once you outgrow the built-in widget set or want capabilities ratatui deliberately
doesn't include itself.

## tachyonfx — animations and effects

Composable animation/transition effects layered on top of ratatui's normal rendering —
covered in depth in [Animations & Effects](/ratatui/animations-and-effects/). The right
choice once manual tick-based state updates stop being enough (fades, wipes, glitch effects,
sequenced/parallel effect composition).

```bash
cargo add tachyonfx
```

## ratzilla — ratatui in the browser (WASM)

Compiles ratatui apps to WebAssembly and renders them in a normal web page (via an HTML
canvas or terminal emulator embed), letting you ship a ratatui UI as a website with no server
component running the actual TUI. The Tachyonfx effects playground mentioned in
[Animations & Effects](/ratatui/animations-and-effects/) is itself built this way.

## mousefood — embedded / no_std backend

A `Backend` implementation targeting embedded displays rather than a terminal emulator,
built to work with ratatui's `no_std` support (added in 0.30). Used to run ratatui UIs
directly on microcontroller displays (ESP32, STM32, and similar), and even more unusual
targets like the PSP handheld console, entirely without an OS-level terminal underneath.

## cargo-generate templates

```bash
cargo install --locked cargo-generate
cargo generate ratatui/templates
```

Official starting-point templates — a minimal "simple" template and a more structured
"component" template implementing the [Component Architecture](/ratatui/application-architecture/)
pattern out of the box, including async event handling, config loading, and CLI argument
parsing already wired up.

## Where to find more

- **Showcase** (`ratatui.rs/showcase/`) — real apps built with ratatui, and a curated list of
  third-party widget crates beyond the ones above.
- **Ratatui Forum** (`forum.ratatui.rs`) and **Discord** — for questions specific to your
  app's design that go beyond this reference.
- **`awesome-ratatui`** on GitHub — a community-maintained curated list, useful for
  discovering widget crates for specific niches (markdown rendering, syntax highlighting,
  file trees, image display in-terminal, etc) that aren't part of ratatui core and aren't
  covered in depth here.

Project.FAQ:
# FAQ

**Does ratatui require any system libraries (ncurses, etc)?**
No. With the default Crossterm backend, ratatui + Crossterm are 100% pure Rust with zero C
dependencies. On Arch Linux, `cargo add ratatui crossterm` is the entire installation step —
no `pacman -S` for anything TUI-related.

**Why doesn't my `Paragraph` scroll automatically?**
Ratatui doesn't do automatic scrolling — you track a scroll offset in your own state and
pass it to `.scroll((y, x))` on the widget each frame. See
[Scrolling Content](/ratatui/scrolling-content/).

**Why is my terminal broken/garbled after my app crashed?**
Almost always a missing terminal-restore step on the panic/error path. Use
`ratatui::run()` or `ratatui::init()`/`ratatui::restore()` (see
[Terminal Setup](/ratatui/terminal-setup/)), which install a panic hook that restores the
terminal automatically — if you're doing fully manual setup, make sure your own equivalent
runs on every exit path, panics included. If your terminal is already stuck, run `reset` or
`stty sane` in the broken shell.

**Why did my keypress fire my action twice?**
You're not filtering for `KeyEventKind::Press`. Some terminals report both press and release
key events; without the check you'll often see a handler run twice per physical keypress. See
[Handling Input](/ratatui/handling-input/).

**How do I animate things?**
There's no built-in animation system — advance numeric state on a timer (via
`event::poll(timeout)`) and let `draw` render whatever the current state says, every tick.
See [Animations & Effects](/ratatui/animations-and-effects/), and consider `tachyonfx` for
anything beyond simple linear ticking.

**`Block::title()` used to take a `Title` — what happened to it?**
As of 0.30, `Block::title()` accepts anything convertible into a `Line` directly, and the old
`widgets::block::Title` type was removed — alignment now lives on the `Line` itself
(`Line::from("...").centered()`). See [Block](/ratatui/block-widget/).

**What's the difference between `ratatui`, `ratatui-core`, and `ratatui-widgets`?**
As an application author, always depend on plain `ratatui` — it re-exports everything. The
split into `ratatui-core`/`ratatui-widgets`/backend crates (since 0.30) exists mainly for
third-party widget-library authors who want a more stable API surface to build against. See
[Choosing a Backend](/ratatui/choosing-a-backend/).

**Can I use ratatui without Crossterm?**
Yes — Termion (Unix-only) and Termwiz are both supported as alternative backends via feature
flags. See [Choosing a Backend](/ratatui/choosing-a-backend/).

**Does ratatui support `no_std` / embedded targets?**
Yes, as of 0.30, with `default-features = false`. You'll need a custom or third-party
`Backend` implementation (e.g. `mousefood`) since there's no terminal underneath on bare
metal. See [The Ratatui Ecosystem](/ratatui/the-ratatui-ecosystem/).

**How do I test a ratatui app without a real terminal?**
`TestBackend` renders into an in-memory buffer you can assert against directly, and pairs
well with `insta` snapshot testing for anything beyond trivial output. See
[Testing Ratatui Apps](/ratatui/testing-ratatui-apps/).
Project.Migrating Between Versions:
# Migrating Between Versions

Ratatui is under active development and does periodically ship breaking changes (it hasn't
reached 1.0 yet), documented in the project's `BREAKING-CHANGES.md` on GitHub for every
release. This page summarizes the changes most likely to affect an existing app moving to
0.30, the current release line as of this writing.

## Coming from tui-rs (the pre-fork library)

If you're working from an old tutorial referencing `tui` rather than `ratatui`, note that
`tui-rs` was abandoned by its original author and forked into `ratatui` in 2023, which has
been the actively maintained continuation ever since — `tui` should be treated as
unmaintained/legacy, and any new project should start on `ratatui` directly rather than
migrating later.

## Migrating to 0.30

- **Modular crates**: application code is unaffected — keep depending on plain `ratatui`.
  Only widget-library authors need to consider switching internal imports to `ratatui-core`.
  See [Choosing a Backend](/ratatui/choosing-a-backend/).
- **`Block::title()`**: now takes `Into<Line>` instead of the removed `block::Title` type;
  set alignment on the `Line` itself (`Line::from("...").centered()`) instead of a separate
  `Title` builder. See [Block](/ratatui/block-widget/).
- **`Alignment` renamed**: to `HorizontalAlignment` (a `VerticalAlignment` type was also
  added). Update `use ratatui::layout::Alignment` to `HorizontalAlignment`.
- **`List::highlight_symbol`**: now takes `Into<Line>` instead of `&str` — wrap existing
  string-literal calls if you relied on implicit conversion, and note this can no longer be
  called in a `const` context since `Into::into` isn't `const`.
- **`Style` no longer implements `Styled`**, but `Stylize` shorthand methods (`.red()`,
  `.bold()`, etc) are now implemented directly on `Style`, enabling `const` style
  definitions like `const ERR: Style = Style::new().red();` — see
  [Style Basics](/ratatui/style-basics/).
- **Custom `Backend` implementations**: now require an associated `Error` type and a
  `clear_region` method; generic code written against `Backend` needs its error type updated
  accordingly. Only relevant if you wrote your own backend rather than using
  Crossterm/Termion/Termwiz.
- **`WidgetRef`**: no longer has a blanket `Widget` impl; the blanket relationship is
  reversed (`Widget` is now blanket-implemented for `&W` where `W: Widget`). Widgets that
  implemented `WidgetRef` directly should implement `Widget` for a reference type instead.
- **`Marker` enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`**: exhaustive `match` statements over
  `symbols::Marker` (e.g. for `Canvas`/`Chart`) need a wildcard `_` arm added, since new
  marker variants (`Quadrant`, `Sextant`, `Octant`) were added in this release and more may
  be added later without that counting as a breaking change.
- **MSRV bump**: 0.30 requires Rust 1.86.0 or later, and the codebase itself moved to the
  Rust 2024 edition.

## General upgrade advice

1. Read `CHANGELOG.md` and `BREAKING-CHANGES.md` on the
   [ratatui GitHub repo](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) for the specific version jump
   you're making — don't assume this page (covering the 0.30 jump specifically) transfers to
   whatever the current release is by the time you read this.
2. Bump one minor version at a time rather than jumping several releases at once if your app
   is large; `cargo build` errors after each bump tend to point directly at the exact
   breaking change involved.
3. Re-run your test suite (see [Testing Ratatui Apps](/ratatui/testing-ratatui-apps/)) after
   each bump — snapshot tests in particular are good at catching subtle rendering-output
   changes that wouldn't otherwise show up as a compile error.
Project.Community and Resources:
# Community and Resources

Official links for going deeper than this reference, or for getting unstuck on something
specific to your app.

## Official documentation

- **Website** — <https://ratatui.rs/> — concepts, tutorials, recipes, and the widget/example
  galleries this guide draws from.
- **API docs** — <https://docs.rs/ratatui/latest/ratatui/> — the full generated Rust API
  reference, always current for whatever version you have pinned in `Cargo.toml`.
- **Examples repository** — widget-level copy-paste examples and full example apps, linked
  from the website's Examples section.
- **Changelog** — `CHANGELOG.md` in the GitHub repo, generated from Conventional Commits.
- **Breaking Changes** — `BREAKING-CHANGES.md` in the GitHub repo — check this before
  upgrading a pinned version, see [Migrating Between Versions](/ratatui/migrating-between-versions/).

## Getting help

- **Discord** — the most active place for real-time questions.
- **Matrix** — bridged with Discord, `#ratatui:matrix.org`.
- **Ratatui Forum** (`forum.ratatui.rs`) — better for longer-form/searchable questions than
  chat.
- **GitHub Issues** — for actual bugs and feature requests against ratatui itself, not
  general "how do I build X" questions (those fit Discord/Forum better).

## Contributing

- Read the contributing guidelines in the GitHub repo before opening a pull request.
- Ratatui accepts AI-assisted contributions but has specific guidelines for it — read the
  "AI Contributions" section of `CONTRIBUTING.md` before submitting AI-generated code.

## Showcase

- **Showcase** (`ratatui.rs/showcase/`) — real published apps built with ratatui, plus a
  built-in-widgets gallery and a third-party widgets gallery.
- **`awesome-ratatui`** on GitHub — community-curated list of apps and libraries, useful for
  finding prior art before building something from scratch (markdown rendering, file
  pickers, image previews, syntax highlighting, and other common TUI needs that fall outside
  ratatui's own scope).

## License

Ratatui is dual-licensed (MIT / Apache-2.0), matching common Rust ecosystem convention — check
the `LICENSE-MIT`/`LICENSE-APACHE` files in the repository for the exact terms before
depending on it in a project with specific licensing requirements.
